text.en: Children and their teacher are cleaning a park on National Cleanliness Day. Why? Have you seen piles of waste near your home or school? Today we find out how waste is made and how we can take charge of it.

We make a lot of waste in our everyday activities. We throw away old clothes, tins, bottles, paper, vegetable and fruit peels, plastic wrappers, pencil shavings, old batteries and much more. Packaged products, take-away food, plastic and decorations all create waste. We try to throw waste away, but it often ends up in garbage piles near our homes, schools and neighbourhoods. How do we feel about this, and can we do something about it? Managing waste is in our own hands.
Trash lying on the roadside can harm animals, because cows and other animals can die by eating plastic mixed with food. Some people burn plastic, which gives out harmful gases. People fall ill because of the garbage around them. Puddles and wastewater flowing through roads bring mosquitoes whose bites can cause diseases, and the wastewater may carry germs. But in some places people have worked hard to clean their houses and surroundings, and we can learn from them.
The first rule is to REDUCE the amount of waste we make. Many people avoid food and drinks packed in wrappers or plastic bottles, and carry cloth bags instead of plastic bags. The more things we buy, the more we throw away, so we should buy only what we need and use it until it is no longer usable. We can share old toys and books with children who need them and cannot afford to buy them.
The second rule is to REUSE things instead of throwing them away. Our grandparents made quilts and bags from old sarees and clothes, and gave old clothes to those in need. We can wrap gifts in newspaper or old cloth, which saves resources and adds a personal touch. We can use paper used on one side for rough work, refill a steel or copper bottle instead of buying new ones, and make toys and decorations from old newspapers, calendars, bottles and boxes. We can even make a paper bag from newspaper with no scissors and no glue, and give a thank-you gift made from waste to the person who keeps our locality clean.
Silluk, a village in Arunachal Pradesh, has clean roads and tree-lined streets that feel like a garden. It won an award and is called a zero waste village because it manages its waste so well. Chhota Narena was one of the first villages to become waste-free. Cities like Indore and Mysuru are known for being clean. We can ask our elders about a clean village or town they know, and find out about the Swachh Bharat Mission.
We often see dustbins of two colours at schools, markets, parks, bus stands, railway platforms and melas. The green dustbin is for things that rot easily and mix with soil, like dried leaves, fruit peels, vegetable waste and egg shells. Waste in the green bin can be turned into compost, which is food for plants and for tiny animals in the soil. The blue dustbin is for things made of metal, glass, plastic and paper, which can be made into new objects. This is called recycling. Some villages keep separate bins for each material so it is easier to send them for recycling. Sharp things like broken glass or needles should be wrapped in cloth and paper so sanitation workers are not hurt.
Each of us can help keep our home, school, neighbourhood, city and country clean. We can keep our room tidy and learn the names of cleaning tools like brooms, mops and dustpans. On National Cleanliness Day, 30 January, we can take a pledge to keep ourselves and our surroundings clean. Our aim is Want not, Waste not.

problem.en: Which dustbin do these go in: onion peels, plastic bottle, eggshell, paper, light bulb, rotten fruit?

text.en: Onion peels rot easily, so they go in the green dustbin.

why.en: Green is for things that rot and make compost.

text.en: Eggshells and rotten fruit also go in the green dustbin.

why.en: They are natural waste that mixes with soil.

text.en: Plastic bottle and paper go in the blue dustbin.
A light bulb is glass, so it goes in the blue dustbin, wrapped carefully if broken.

why.en: Glass can be recycled and broken glass can hurt workers.

text.en: Use cloth or reusable plates and cups instead of plastic ones.
Wrap gifts in newspaper or old cloth.
Share extra food and put peels in the green dustbin.

problem.en: List three ways to reduce waste at home.

text.en: Carry a cloth bag to the shop.
Refill a steel bottle instead of buying new ones.
Use paper on both sides and share old toys and books.

prompt.en: Tell a friend what reduce, reuse and the two dustbins mean.

requiredIdeas.en: Reduce means making less waste by buying only what we need
Reuse means using things again instead of throwing them away
Green dustbin is for things that rot and become compost
Blue dustbin is for metal, glass, plastic and paper that can be recycled

commonMisconceptions.en: All waste goes in one dustbin
Burning plastic is a good way to get rid of it

points.en: Waste is made by our everyday activities and we can manage it ourselves.
Garbage and wastewater cause illness, mosquitoes and harm to animals.
Reduce and reuse are the first two rules.
The green dustbin is for waste that rots into compost; the blue one is for materials that can be recycled.
Villages like Silluk show that a clean place is possible; our aim is Want not, Waste not.
